evidence.text: A child in a wrap, with outstretched arms but bundled legs
Pictograph of a small child with its two arms outstretched.
十一月，陽气動，萬物滋，人以爲偁。象形。凡子之屬皆从子。(李陽冰曰：“子在襁緥中，足併也。”)

Characters in the same phonetic series (子) (Zhengzhang, 2003)
Pictogram (象形) – an image of a baby, with a large head and spread arms. The legs are wrapped in a blanket. Compare with 了, where the arms are wrapped, and 㜽, in which a lock of hair is visible on top. Compare also 棄 and 毓, in which the image of the baby is reversed upside-down.
The big seal script form is much more elaborate, showing a baby with hair on a head (囟) and arms on the two sides of the body, sitting on a stool (几).
See also the right component of 保.
;child
:Cognate with 字 (OC *zlɯs, “character; letter”), 慈 (OC *zɯ, “loving; kind”), 滋 (OC *ʔsɯ, “to grow, to breed, to propagate, to bring about, to increase”), 孳 (OC *ʔsɯ, *zɯs, “to breed, to propagate”).
;first earthly branch
:Smith (2011) proposes the first earthly branch had been 甾. Observing that 甾 is closely linked with 緇 (“dark, stained”), 淄 (“murky (water)”), 菑 (zī, “field cleared by burning”) (all pronounced *tsrə), he proposes that initially the first earthly branch 甾 (OC *ts[r]əʔ) had meant "darkened, voided, the darkened stage" and had denoted the new moon phase (ibid.). Meanwhile, 子 (OC tsəʔ) had originated from a Sino-Tibetan root meaning "to come forth" and had denoted the moon's "coming forth" stage (i.e. early waning-gibbous phase) (ibid.).
:Sometime in Warring States period, a change occurred that 子 became the first earthly branch and 巳 (OC *s-ləʔ) filled the void of the sixth earthly branch (Matsumaru, 2015), "due to phonological closeness (combined with the semantic opacity of the Branch terms at later eras)" (Smith, 2011).
:Association with the rat was possibly arbitrary, analogous to how 辰, the fifth earthly branch, was arbitrarily associated with the dragon (Ferlus, 2013).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The source describes two Shang-era forms: 𢀈, with hair and two legs, and 子, with a large infant head, moving arms and undeveloped legs. It identifies the graph’s original sense as “infant.” It says the more elaborate form was used for the first earthly branch and was gradually replaced after the beginning of the Zhou period by 子; the simpler 子 form was used for a child and for the sixth branch, corresponding to later 巳. It also reports that Heji 94’s 有子 refers to pregnancy, and that 子 could designate a same-surname Shang clan leader. These are the database’s readings of the evidence, not direct observations made in this research.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：子

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 甲骨部件分析 / 子 / cited inscription examples
evidence.text: The entry cites Heji 94, 有子, for a pregnancy-related use; it also cites Western Zhou bronze inscriptions in which 子 is used loanwise for 慈 in the Yu ding and 孜 in the Shiqiang pan. The latter are graph-borrowing examples and do not show that those words share the pictorial origin of 子.
evidence.kind: inscription examples as reported by a secondary database
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：子

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 甲骨部件分析 / 子 / disputed branch history
evidence.text: This account assigns the early first-branch use to 𢀈 and the sixth-branch use to 子, with 子 later replacing 𢀈 for the first branch and 巳 taking over the sixth. A different proposal summarized in the opened Wiktionary entry identifies 甾 as the original first branch and gives a Warring States reassignment account. These are competing reconstructions of branch history; the sources do not establish one uncontested sequence here.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：子

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, text of 《說文解字》 and 段玉裁’s commentary
evidence.text: The entry gives 許慎’s Han-era explanation: 子 is associated with the eleventh month, the stirring of yang and the growth of things; it classifies the graph as 象形. It also records 𡿹 as an ancient form and a 籀文 form described with 囟, hair, arms, legs and 几. 段玉裁 explains the month-and-growth passage through 子 as a conventional designation and interprets the graph as depicting growth and human limbs. This is historical lexicographic interpretation, not evidence that the seasonal explanation is the graph’s original Shang meaning.
evidence.kind: primary lexicographic text with later commentary
evidence.title: 說文解字「子」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 甲骨部件分析 / 子 / later extensions
evidence.text: The entry reports a child-related base sense, a Shang use for a clan leader, and Warring States Chu-slip use in 君子, where 子 functions as a suffix for a person. It also reports later use for “young/immature,” as in 子薑. This supports distinct attested uses, but does not by itself date every semantic transition or establish a complete chain from child to honorific to suffix.
evidence.kind: lexical history as reported by a secondary database
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：子

Its branch section summarizes both the account involving an earlier graph and Smith’s proposal involving 甾; it is useful here as evidence that analyses differ, not as independent primary paleographic evidence.

evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 / 子 / form and function history
evidence.text: The page distinguishes two Shang forms: 𢀈, described as a newborn with hair and two legs, and 子, emphasizing a large infant head, moving arms, and undeveloped legs; it identifies the graph’s original sense as “infant.” It reports the more complex form for the first earthly branch and its replacement by 子 after the beginning of Zhou, while 子 also represented a child and the sixth branch, later written 巳. It cites Heji 94 有子 as a pregnancy-related example and describes later clan-leader, loan, suffix, and ‘young’ uses. These are the database’s interpretations and reported attestations, not direct readings independently verified here.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The browser returned an internal error for the requested official Unicode Unihan character page. The supplied local kMandarin row was checked, and the official Unicode proposal was inspected, but the character record itself could not be verified.
No primary online Baxter–Sagart table page was verified. The two exact 子 readings are transcribed from the supplied local table rows 4903 and 4905, with MC and OC notation kept separate.

The opened paleographic account dates the forms by inscription corpus and period but does not provide an independently verified calendar date for the earliest child-sense token. Heji 94 is a cited Shang oracle-bone example, but the exact reading and interpretation are those reported by the database.

Accounts differ over which graph represented the first branch before 子 took that position, and over the timing and mechanism of the reassignment. The evidence inspected here does not resolve the disagreement.

The graph’s pictorial interpretation as an infant is well supported by the inspected paleographic account, but its proposed anatomical details vary across authorities. No glyph image was visually inspected in this research.

The Shuowen seasonal explanation is a Han lexicographic account; it should not be treated as proof that 子’s original graphic meaning was “growth,” nor as a dated lexical attestation of every child-related sense.

No evidence gathered here establishes a full semantic chronology from child to offspring, honorific, suffix, or seed/fruit. The latter definition in the dossier is not independently dated by the inspected pages.

The exact date of the earliest child-sense inscription was not established. The CUHK page reports Shang examples and inscription references but no independently verified calendar date for the earliest 子 child token.
The paleographic account supports a pictorial infant interpretation, but the anatomical details are source interpretations; no artifact photograph or glyph pixels were visually inspected here.

The relationship and chronology among the first-branch graph, 子, and the later sixth-branch graph 巳 remain contested in the dossier’s sources; the opened CUHK page gives one account and does not resolve competing analyses.

The broader semantic chain from child to offspring, honorific, suffix, and seed/fruit is not fully dated or established by the inspected pages. The CUHK entry reports several discrete uses, not a complete chronology.
The Xiaoxuetang 子.6 page failed to open and the applicable official image-rights notice was not verified, so no Xiaoxuetang image is proposed.
The Commons original SVG URL was recovered from the exact file page, but the browser rejected its SVG content type, so image pixels were not visually inspected.
